paras: The threatened lynching of George Williams and Charles Crandall followed the arrest of the two men, one described as "colored" and the other as white, on charges of breaking into the home of an elderly couple outside Middletown, Connecticut, near Durham, on October 23, 1888, and assaulting the wife. A New Haven wire dispatch reported "threats of lynching them," but no crowd or move against the prisoners appears in the coverage. Both men were indicted for rape and in December were sentenced to fifteen years in state prison.

Thomas Schorkowski, a 77-year-old native of Poland, lived with his wife, aged 67, near the Pine Grove cemetery in Middletown on the road to Durham, about three miles from the city. Williams and Crandall were wood choppers.

About 2 a.m. on Tuesday, October 23, two men smashed in the door, seized Mrs. Schorkowski from her bed and carried her outside, where both were accused of raping her. Her husband was knocked senseless with a club when he tried to rescue her, a blow the Waterbury Evening Democrat and a fuller New Haven wire attributed to Crandall. Newspapers blamed drink, and the Waterbury paper noted an empty bottle left at the scene.

A neighbor, named in Waterbury as Edwin J. Roberts, went to Middletown to inform the police. Chief of Police Chapman and an officer tracked the two men to a wood-chopper's shanty on the Dooley farm near the Durham line, where they were found playing cards. They were handcuffed, taken back to the Schorkowski house to be identified and then locked up.

The short New Haven wire, dated October 24, closed with the line "There are threats of lynching them," and the Alexandria Gazette's longer version said the case had "created intense excitement in the vicinity." None of the reports from Middletown itself mentions a threat, a crowd or any move on the lockup.

On October 24 the two men were examined in the Middletown police court, where Mrs. Schorkowski, "unable to walk without assistance," testified against them. Both were bound over to the November term of the Superior Court under bonds of $2,500 each and taken to the Haddam jail. On November 14 a grand jury at Middletown, instructed by Judge Fenn, found a true bill against them for rape. The Springfield Weekly Republican reported on December 7 that Crandall and Williams had been sentenced at the Middletown superior court to 15 years in state prison for rape.

The story spread in two versions of a New Haven wire: a short item printed from Waterbury and Wilmington to Rock Island and Lehighton, and a longer narrative carried by the Alexandria Gazette, the Omaha Bee and Vermont's United Opinion. Only the short version mentioned lynching. Headline writers treated that line differently: the Camden Evening Telegram titled the item "Two Brutes Escape Lynching," while the Omaha Bee headed its version "Lynching Too Good For Them" even though its text reported no threat.

Other headlines dwelt on the crime, from "Fiendish Assault Near Middletown" in the New York Evening World to "They Are Worse Than Brutes" in Waterbury and "A Horrible Atrocity" in Vermont. The accused were called "fiends," "ruffians," "brutes" and "scoundrels," while the Waterbury paper described the couple as "worthy." Every paper identified Williams as "colored" and Crandall as white, but none presented the threat or the crime in racial terms. Connecticut papers followed the case through the police court and grand jury, and the sentence appeared in a Springfield weekly's state news column.

Wire reports placed the house "near Durham" and credited "the Durham police" with the arrest, while the Middletown and Waterbury accounts put it in Middletown on the Durham road and named Middletown's Chief Chapman. The local accounts are the stronger evidence, since the neighbor reported to the Middletown police and the case was heard in Middletown's police court. The grand jury report dated the crime October 22, against the early Tuesday morning of October 23 given in the first reports.

framing.detail: The short wire carried the threat line flatly; the Camden Evening Telegram headed it 'Two Brutes Escape Lynching'.
The Omaha Bee headed its special telegram 'Lynching Too Good For Them', endorsing the sentiment though its text reported no threat.
Local Connecticut papers condemned the crime ('They Are Worse Than Brutes', 'Wretches Found Guilty') and reported the legal process without mention of lynching.
